1.pericope_label: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bare him no children: and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar — and Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the Lord hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her. And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai

schools.summary: Begin with the composition. The history of Abram is given in a succession of brief narratives, written possibly by the patriarch himself; and though papyrus was known at Ur, the absence of any convenient writing material for ordinary use would oblige men in those ancient days to content themselves with short inscriptions, like the tablets of clay brought from Ur, many of which are said to be considerably older than the time of Abram. The narrator would naturally make but few alterations in such precious documents, and hence a certain amount of recapitulation, as in the Books of Samuel, where again we have not a narrative from one pen but the arrangement of materials already ancient. Since the divine object was the revealing to mankind of the way by which God would raise up man from the fall, the narrator would be guided by inspiration in his choice of materials and in the omission of what did not fall in with that purpose; and the evident reverence with which he deals with these records is a warrant to us of their genuineness. Such additions as the remark that one valley was many centuries later called the King’s Dale are generally acknowledged to have been the work of Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue, after the return from the exile. On the name, note that as it apparently comes from the Arabic verb to flee, it cannot have been her original name, unless we suppose she really was an Arab fugitive who had taken refuge in Egypt; more probably she was an Egyptian woman who had escaped to Abram when he was in the Negeb, and had then received this appellation, which virtually means run-away. On the idiom, render it that I may be builded by her, and trace the words for son, daughter, house and to build to the same Hebrew root, the idea being that the children build the house and give a man the pledge of continuance — until late times the tent was the habitation while the house was the family, so that to build a man a sure house meant to give him lasting prosperity, whence too the close connection between building and the bestowal of children in the Psalms. Since the children of a woman bestowed by her mistress upon the husband were regarded as belonging to the wife, Sarah, despairing of bearing a son herself at seventy-five and after ten years in Canaan, concluded that her heir was to be born of a substitute. As regards the morality of the act, note that marriage with one wife was the original law, and that when polygamy was introduced it was coupled by the inspired narrator with violence and licence; monogamy was the rule, as we see in the households of Noah, Terah and Isaac, but many allowed themselves a greater latitude, and in so doing their conduct falls below the level of Christian morality. Everyone’s actions are strongly influenced by the general views of the people among whom he lives; and in Abram’s case it must be said in his defence that, with so much depending on his having offspring, he took no steps to obtain another wife but remained content with the barren Sarai, and that when he did take Hagar it was at his wife’s request, for a reason which seemed to them adequate and even religious. Elsewhere note that Abram gave Sarai full power to act as mistress toward her maid, without raising the slave who was made a concubine above her position; but that as soon as Sarai made her feel that power, Hagar fled — so that instead of securing the fulfilment of their wishes they reaped nothing but grief and vexation, and apparently lost the maid through their self-concerted scheme, until the faithful covenant God turned the whole into a blessing.

Note that she is before said to be barren and he to be childless; that God had promised him a seed but as yet he had none, which was a trial of his faith; that she was his wife when they came out of Ur, that they stayed some time at Haran, and that they had now been ten years in Canaan, being seventy-five and eighty-five, so that there was no great probability of having children — wherefore the following step was taken. Render her words the Lord hath shut me up, that is her womb, as the wombs of the house of Abimelech were shut; she now despaired of children at this age, perceiving that it had ceased to be with her after the manner of women, and she refers this to the will and power of God, for as children are his gift and an heritage from him, so it is his pleasure sometimes to withhold this blessing from those who greatly desire it. Then take the history at large. Sarai, through the impatience of long delay, resorted to a method of obtaining seed by her husband at variance with the word of God; seeing herself barren and past the age of bearing, she inferred the necessity of a new remedy, in order that Abram might obtain the promised blessing. Note expressly that the design of marrying a second wife did not originate with Abram but with Sarai, to teach us that the holy man was not impelled by lust to these nuptials, but that when he was thinking of no such thing he was induced to engage in them by the exhortation of his wife. Ask then whether Sarai substituted her handmaid in her place through the mere desire of having offspring: so it seems to some, yet it is incredible that the pious matron should not have been cognizant of those promises so often repeated to her husband, and it ought to be taken for granted among all pious persons that the mother of the people of God was a participator of the same grace with her husband. Sarai therefore does not desire offspring from a merely natural impulse, but yields her conjugal rights to another through a wish to obtain the benediction she knew was divinely promised — not making a divorce from her husband, but assigning him another wife from whom he might receive children. And certainly if she had desired offspring in the ordinary manner, it would rather have come into her mind to do it by the adoption of a son than by giving place to a second wife, for we know the vehemence of female jealousy. Note also that Sarai claims for herself, by right of dominion, the child which Hagar shall bring forth, because handmaids do not bring forth for themselves, having no power over their own body; and that by first speaking to her husband she does not offer him a concubine who should be as a harlot, but a wife. Hence it appears that when persons are wiser in their own eyes than they ought to be, they easily fall into the snare of trying illicit means: the desire of Sarai proceeds from the zeal of faith, but because it is not so subjected to God as to wait his time, she immediately has recourse to polygamy, which is nothing else than the corruption of lawful marriage. And since Sarai, that holy woman, fanned in her husband the same flame of impatience with which she burned, learn how diligently we ought to be on our guard lest Satan should surprise us by some secret fraud; for not only does he induce wicked men openly to oppose our faith, but sometimes, privately and by stealth, he assails us through the medium of good and simple men, that he may overcome us unawares.

Call this the marriage of Abram to Hagar, who was his secondary wife; and say that herein, though some excuse may be made for him, he cannot be justified, for from the beginning it was not so, and when it was so it seems to have proceeded from an irregular desire to build up families for the speedier peopling of the world and the church. Certainly it must not be so now: Christ has reduced this matter to the first institution, and makes the marriage union to be between one man and one woman only. Then observe who made the match — would one think it? — Sarai herself. From which note first, that it is the policy of Satan to tempt us by our nearest and dearest relations, or those friends of whom we have a good opinion and for whom we have an affection; the temptation is most dangerous when it is sent by a hand that is least suspected, and it is our wisdom therefore to consider, not so much who speaks, as what is spoken. Note second, that God’s commands consult our comfort and honour much better than our own contrivances do: it would have been much more for Sarai’s interest if Abram had kept to the rule of God’s law instead of being guided by her foolish projects, but we often do ill for ourselves. Then observe the inducement, which was Sarai’s barrenness. She was very fair, a very agreeable and dutiful wife, and a sharer with him in his large possessions, and yet written childless — whence note that God dispenses his gifts variously, loading us with benefits but not overloading us, since some cross or other is appointed to be an alloy to great enjoyments; and that the mercy of children is often given to the poor and denied to the rich.

Give the chapter its argument first: Sarai, having no child, gives Hagar her maid to Abram for wife; she conceives and despises her mistress; Sarai is offended and upbraids Abram; Abram vindicates himself, and Hagar, being hardly used, runs away; she is met by an angel and counselled to return; God promises greatly to multiply her seed, gives the name of Ishmael to the child, and shows his disposition and character; Hagar calls the name of the Lord who spoke to her, Thou God seest me, and calls the name of the well Beer-lahai-roi; and Ishmael is born in the eighty-sixth year of Abram’s age. Then note that as Hagar was an Egyptian, a Greek father’s conjecture is very probable, that she was one of those female slaves whom Pharaoh gave to Abram when he sojourned in Egypt; and that her name signifies a stranger or sojourner, which she likely got in the family of Abram, the word being pure Hebrew. On the giving of the maid, remember that female slaves constituted a part of the private patrimony or possessions of a wife, and that she had a right, according to the usages of those times, to dispose of them as she pleased, the husband having no authority in the case; and that the slave being the absolute property of the mistress, not only her person but the fruits of her labour, with all her children, were her owner’s property also, so that the children born of the slave were considered as the children of the mistress. It was on this ground that Sarai gave her slave to Abram; and we find what must necessarily be the consequence in all cases of polygamy, that strifes and contentions took place. Elsewhere say, more briefly, that herein, though he may be excused, he cannot be justified, for from the beginning it was not so.

debates: What the name Hagar means and where she came from.
Whether Sarai acted from natural desire or from faith in the promise.
How far Abram can be excused for taking a second wife.
What the phrase rendered obtain children by her properly means.
How the narratives of Abram came to be written and arranged.
outliers: Ellicott derives Hagar from an Arabic verb to flee and makes the name mean run-away; Clarke derives it from a Hebrew word for stranger.
Ellicott gives an account of clay tablets, papyrus at Ur, and later editorial additions by Ezra, inside a commentary on the verse.
Calvin argues that a merely natural desire for a child would have led Sarai to adopt rather than to admit a rival.
Calvin locates the fault precisely: the desire proceeded from the zeal of faith, but would not wait God’s time.
Ellicott pleads in Abram’s defence that he took no step of his own toward another wife.
Henry warns that Satan tempts through the hand least suspected, so we should weigh what is spoken rather than who speaks.
Clarke sets out the property law by which a slave’s children belonged to the mistress and not to the husband.

3.pericope_label: And Sarai Abram’s wife took Hagar her maid the Egyptian, after Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to her husband Abram to be his wife — and he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes — and Sarai said unto Abram, My wrong be upon thee: the Lord judge between me and thee

schools.summary: State what the design of Sarai was: neither did she intend to make her house a brothel, nor to be the betrayer of her maid’s chastity, nor a pander for her husband. Yet Hagar is improperly called a wife, because she was brought into another person’s bed against the law of God; wherefore let us know that this connection was so far illicit as to be something between fornication and marriage. The same thing takes place with all those inventions which are appended to the word of God: with whatever fair pretext they may be covered, there is an inherent corruption which degenerates from the purity of the word and vitiates the whole. Then relate how the punishment of excessive precipitancy quickly followed. The chief blame rested with Sarai, yet because Abram had proved himself too credulous God chastises both as they deserve: Sarai is grievously and bitterly tried by the proud contempt of her handmaid, Abram is harassed by unjust complaints, and thus both pay the penalty of their levity, while the contrivance devised by Sarai and too eagerly embraced by Abram fails of success. Meanwhile in Hagar an instance of ingratitude is set before us, since she, having been treated with singular kindness and honour, begins to hold her mistress in contempt; and since this is an exceedingly common disease of the mind, let the faithful accustom themselves to the endurance of it, if at any time so unjust a return be made for their acts of kindness. But especially let the infirmity of Sarai move us, since she was unable to bear the contempt of her maid. It was part of her punishment that she was brought so low as to forget herself for a while, and, being vehemently excited, conducted herself with so much weakness. To the utmost of her power she had impelled her husband to act rashly, and now she petulantly insults him, although innocent; for she adduces nothing for which Abram was to be blamed, but reproaches him with the fact that she had given her maid into his bosom, and complains that she is condemned by this maid, without having first ascertained whether he intended to assist the bad cause by his countenance or not. Thus blind is the assault of anger: it rushes impetuously hither and thither, and condemns without inquiry those who are entirely free from blame. If ever any woman was of a meek and gentle spirit, Sarai excelled in that virtue; whereas therefore we see her patience violently shaken by a single offence, let every one of us be so much the more resolved to govern his own passions. Note also that she makes improper use of the name of God and almost forgets the reverence enforced on the godly: she makes her appeal to the judgment of God, and what else is this than to call down destruction on her own head? For if God had interposed as judge, he must of necessity have executed punishment upon one or other of them; but Abram had done no injury, and it remains therefore that she must have felt the vengeance of God, whose anger she had so rashly imprecated upon herself or her husband. Elsewhere note that Sarai took Hagar by the hand, it is probable, and led her into the apartment where Abram was, and presented her to him; that their characters are exactly described and the contrast beautifully given, that the affair might be the more remarkable; and that Sarai applies to Abram for the redress of her grievance, judging it below her dignity to enter into an altercation with her maid.

Note that Abram was now eighty-five years of age, and that this long delay had not only tried his faith but brought him and Sarai to the conclusion that the promised seed was to be obtained by other means. Then set out the arrangement exactly: Hagar was to be, not Abram’s concubine, but his wife; she was to be Sarai’s representative, and though she would now hold the highest place in the household next to Sarai because of this relation to Abram, yet she would continue to be Sarai’s maid. But no sooner had she conceived than, proud of her superiority over her mistress, she wished to overthrow this arrangement, and at all events acted as if she were Abram’s wife absolutely, and thrust Sarai aside. On the complaint, render it, may the wrong done to me be avenged upon thee; Sarai’s act had been one of self-denial for Abram’s sake, and now that it has led to her being treated insolently she makes Abram answerable for it.

Set out the immediate bad consequences of the unhappy marriage: a great deal of mischief it made quickly, for when we do not well both sin and trouble lie at the door, and we may thank ourselves for the guilt and grief that follow us when we go out of the way of our duty. First, Sarai is despised, and thereby provoked and put into a passion. Hagar no sooner perceives herself with child by her master than she looks scornfully upon her mistress, upbraids her perhaps with her barrenness, insults over her to make her fret, and boasts of the prospect she had of bringing an heir to Abram, to that good land, and to the promise; now she thinks herself a better woman than Sarai, more favoured by heaven and likely to be better beloved by Abram, and therefore she will not submit as she has done. Note first that mean and servile spirits, when favoured and advanced either by God or man, are apt to grow haughty and insolent and to forget their place and origin — it is a hard thing to bear honour aright. Note second that we justly suffer by those whom we have sinfully indulged, and that it is a righteous thing with God to make those the instruments of our trouble whom we have made the instruments of our sin, and to ensnare us in our own evil counsels: this stone will return upon him that rolleth it. Then observe that Abram is clamoured upon and cannot be easy while Sarai is out of humour, and that she upbraids him vehemently and very unjustly charges him with the injury.

Note that there are instances of women in other lands who, being barren, consent to their husbands marrying a second wife for the sake of children, and that second marriages on this account, without consent, are very common there. On the complaint, say it appears to be intended as a reproof to Abram, containing an insinuation that it was his fault she had not been a mother, and that he now carried himself more affectionately toward Hagar than toward her, in consequence of which the slave became petulant; and that to remove all suspicion of this kind Abram delivers Hagar up into her hand, since she was certainly under his protection while his secondary wife, but he restores the right Sarai had given him, to prevent her jealousy and uneasiness. Elsewhere set out the ill consequences: Hagar no sooner perceives herself with child but she looks scornfully upon her mistress, upbraids her perhaps with her barrenness, and insults over her; Sarai falls upon Abram and very unjustly charges him with the injury, suspecting that he countenanced Hagar’s insolence, and, as one not willing to hear what Abram had to say, she rashly appeals to God, the Lord judge between me and thee, as if Abram had refused to right her. When passion is upon the throne, reason is out of doors, and is neither heard nor spoken. Those are not always in the right that are most forward in appealing to God; and rash and bold imprecations are commonly evidences of guilt and a bad cause.

debates: Whether the union with Hagar was a marriage, a concubinage, or something between.
What place Hagar was to hold in the household, and what she claimed.
Whether Sarai’s charge against Abram had any justice in it.
What Sarai was actually asking for when she appealed to God as judge.
Why the scheme failed so quickly.
outliers: Calvin refuses both names for the union and places it between fornication and marriage.
Calvin generalises from it that every invention appended to the word of God carries an inherent corruption.
Ellicott defines Hagar’s position exactly — wife, representative, and still a maid — which is what makes the quarrel intelligible.
Calvin shows that Sarai’s appeal, if granted, must have fallen on herself, since Abram had done no wrong.
Calvin holds up Sarai’s meekness precisely to warn that a single offence overthrew it.
Henry turns the reversal into a rule: the instruments of our sin become the instruments of our trouble.
Wesley warns that readiness to appeal to God is commonly evidence of a bad cause.

6.pericope_label: But Abram said unto Sarai, Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee. And when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face — and the angel of the Lord found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur

schools.summary: Show the greatness of Abram’s humanity and modesty from his answer: he does not quarrel with his wife, and though he has the best cause he does not pertinaciously defend it, but voluntarily dismisses the wife who had been given him. For the sake of restoring peace he does violence to his feelings both as a husband and as a father, since in leaving Hagar to the will of her enraged mistress he does not treat her as his wife, and in a certain way undervalues that object of hope which was conceived in her womb; and it is not to be doubted that he was thus calm in bearing the vehemence of his wife because throughout her whole life he had found her obedient, though it was still a great excellence to restrain his temper under so great an indignity. Then ask how his care for the blessed seed had vanished from his mind: Hagar is great with child, and he hopes that the seed through which the salvation of the world was promised is about to proceed from her — why then does he not set Sarai aside and turn his love and desire the more to Hagar? Truly we hence infer that all human contrivances pass away and vanish in smoke as soon as any grievous temptation is presented. Having taken a wife against the divine command, he thinks the matter is succeeding well when he sees her pregnant, and pleases himself in foolish confidence; but when contention suddenly arises he is at his wit’s end and rejects all hope, or at least forgets it — and the same must necessarily happen to us as often as we attempt anything contrary to the word of God. On the meeting, teach with what clemency the Lord acts toward his own people, although they have deserved severe punishment: as he had previously mitigated the punishment of Abram and Sarai, so now he casts a paternal look upon Hagar, so that his favour is extended to the whole family. He does not indeed altogether spare them, lest he should cherish their vices, but he corrects them with gentle remedies. It is probable that Hagar, in going to the desert of Shur, meditated a return to her own country; yet mention seems to be made of the desert and the wilderness to show that she, being miserably afflicted, wandered from the presence of men till the angel met her. And although the form of the vision is not described, do not doubt that it was clothed in a human body, in which nevertheless manifest tokens of celestial glory were conspicuous. Elsewhere note that this is the first time mention is made of an angel in Scripture, and that it is not to be understood of a created angel but of a divine Person, the uncreated angel, the Word or Son of God, called the Angel of God’s presence and the Angel of the covenant, who often appeared in human form before his incarnation; and set against this the Jewish writers who take the angel to be a man sent of God, one saying he was a prophet of those times, some of the rabbins that he was Shem the son of Noah, and another suggesting that he was a mere man, by comparing the passage with one where a certain man found someone — though the context most clearly confutes that notion and proves him the almighty and omniscient God.

Note that the verb rendered dealt hardly is elsewhere translated afflicted, and that its more exact meaning is that Sarai humbled her, that is, reduced her to her original condition. It was quite right that, as Hagar had abused her elevation, Abram should make her yield to Sarai all due respect and submission; but in making her resume her old position as a slave, Sarai was possibly dealing unkindly with her. Add that in running away Hagar not only showed the untamable love of freedom which Ishmael inherited from her, but apparently was repeating the act from which she had her name. On the place, note that she evidently fled by the usual route leading from Hebron past Beersheba to Egypt; that the wilderness was that of Paran, in which Kadesh was situated; and that the fountain by which she sat was on the road to Shur, a desert on the eastern side of Egypt forming the boundary of the territory of the Ishmaelites and of the Amalekites, and reached by the Israelites soon after crossing the Red Sea.

Note that here is the first mention we have in Scripture of an angel’s appearance. Observe how the angel arrested her in her flight: it should seem she was making toward her own country, for she was in the way to Shur, which lay toward Egypt — and it were well if our afflictions would make us think of our home, the better country. But Hagar was now out of her place, and out of the way of her duty, and going further astray, when the angel found her. Note first that it is a great mercy to be stopped in a sinful way, either by conscience or by providence; and second, that God suffers those who are out of the way to wander a while, so that when they see their folly, and what a loss they have brought themselves to, they may be the better disposed to return — Hagar was not stopped till she was in the wilderness, and had sat down, weary enough, and glad of clear water to refresh herself with. Then observe how he examined her, and that he called her Sarai’s maid, as a check to her pride: though she was Abram’s wife and as such obliged to return, he calls her Sarai’s maid to humble her. Though civility teaches us to call others by their highest titles, humility and wisdom teach us to call ourselves by the lowest.

Say the word implies stripes and hard usage, to bring down the body and humble the mind; and that if the slave was to blame in this business, the mistress is not less liable to censure, since she alone had brought her into those circumstances in which it was natural for her to value herself beyond her mistress. On the answer, note that though Hagar was his wife he would not countenance her in anything disrespectful to Sarai; that those who would keep up peace and love must answer hard accusations gently; and that husbands and wives particularly should endeavour not to be both angry together. Say that when Sarai dealt hardly with her, making her serve with rigour, she not only avoided her wrath for the present but totally deserted her service. Then prove at length that the person here called the angel of the Lord was greater than any created being. First, from his promising to perform what God alone could do and foretelling what God alone could know, which shows a prescience proper to God alone. Second, Hagar considers the person who spoke to her as God, calls him by the divine name and addresses him in the way of worship, which, had he been a created angel, he would have refused. Third, the narrator who relates the transaction calls this angel expressly by the incommunicable name, a name never given to any created being. Fourth, this person is the same who is elsewhere called the redeeming Angel, the Angel of God’s presence, and the Angel of the covenant, and whom the Greek version calls the Angel of the Great Counsel, that is, of redeeming man and filling the earth with righteousness. Fifth, these things cannot be spoken of any human or created being. Elsewhere, more briefly, note that here is the first mention in Scripture of an angel’s appearance, who arrested her in her flight.

debates: Whether the angel of the Lord here is a created angel or a divine Person.
Whether Sarai was within her rights in reducing Hagar to her old position.
Why Abram surrendered Hagar although the promised seed might be hers.
Where Hagar was going, and how far she got.
What the word rendered dealt hardly implies.
outliers: Clarke sets out five numbered proofs that the speaker was more than a created being.
Gill reports and rejects three Jewish readings, including that the angel was Shem the son of Noah.
Calvin declines the identification and reads the meeting as clemency extended to the whole household.
Calvin asks why Abram did not prefer the pregnant Hagar, and infers that contrivances vanish under temptation.
Ellicott divides the case, allowing the demand for respect and questioning the reduction to slavery.
Ellicott ties the flight to his own etymology, making Hagar repeat the act from which she was named.
Henry reads the angel’s form of address as a deliberate check on her pride.

8.pericope_label: And he said, Hagar, Sarai’s maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai — and the angel of the Lord said unto her, Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands — and the angel of the Lord said unto her, I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude

schools.summary: Note that in these divine communications God’s knowledge of all the circumstances is not presumed, but the person visited is led on to tell them, which adds very much to the freshness and poetry of the narrative; here, however, in the address Hagar, Sarai’s maid, the angel at least shows that he is aware who she is, and also reminds her of what she had forgotten, that in bestowing her upon Abram Sarai did not cease to be her mistress. Then make the decisive philological point: the word rendered submit thyself is in Hebrew humble thyself, and is the very verb translated dealt hardly a few verses earlier. The angel therefore commands her to take the position which Sarai was forcing upon her; and by so doing proves to us that there had been no personal maltreatment — commentators have taken that notion, not from the Hebrew, but from the English version. On the promise, state the purpose of the divine manifestation: Abram’s son must not be mixed up with and lost among the debased population of Egypt, but must be the father of a free people; and Hagar will now submit to her lot as a slave, that she may secure liberty for her offspring. Elsewhere run the speeches through in order, and note that in the angel Hagar recognised God manifesting himself to her, the presence of the Lord, and called him a God of seeing.

By the use of this epithet the angel declares that she still remained a servant, though she had escaped the hands of her mistress; because liberty is not to be obtained by stealth, nor by flight, but by manumission. Moreover, by this expression God shows that he approves of civil government, and that the violation of it is inexcusable. The condition of servitude was then hard, and thanks are to be given to the Lord that this barbarity has been abolished; yet God has declared from heaven his pleasure that servants should bear the yoke, as also by the mouth of the apostle he does not give servants their freedom, nor deprive their masters of their use, but only commands them to be kindly and liberally treated. It is to be inferred also, from the circumstance of the time, not only that civil government is to be maintained as a matter of necessity, but that lawful authorities are to be obeyed for conscience’ sake; for although the fugitive Hagar could no longer be compelled to obedience by force, yet her condition was not changed in the sight of God. By the same argument it is proved that if masters at any time deal too hardly with their servants, or if rulers treat their subjects with unjust asperity, their rigour is still to be endured, nor is there just cause for shaking off the yoke, although they may exercise their power too imperiously. Then note the method of the promise: for the purpose of mitigating the offence, and of alleviating what was severe in the precept by some consolation, he promises a blessing in the child she should bear. God might indeed by his own authority have strictly enjoined what was right; but in order that Hagar might the more cheerfully do what she knew to be her duty, he allures her, as by blandishments, to obedience — and to this point those promises tend by which he invites us to voluntary submission, for he would not draw us by servile methods, so that we should obey his commands by constraint, and therefore he mingles mild and paternal invitations with his commands, dealing with us liberally, as with sons. That the angel here promises to do what is peculiar to God alone involves no absurdity, for it is sufficiently usual with God to invest his ministers whom he sends with his own character, that the authority of their word may appear the greater; yet do not disapprove the opinion of most of the ancients, that Christ the Mediator was always present in all the oracles, and that this is the cause why the majesty of God is ascribed to angels. Elsewhere note that he calls her by name, which might surprise her, and describes her by her character and condition, to check her pride and put her in mind of her duty; that it is the same angel throughout, though one rabbi thinks a fresh angel was sent at every speech, and because the phrase is repeated some of the rabbins have fancied there were four angels and others five, but without any reason; and that by what follows he appears to be the Lord himself.

Suppose that the angel, having given Hagar that good counsel, she immediately promised to return and was setting her face homeward, and that then he went on to encourage her with an assurance of the mercy God had in store for her and her seed — for God will meet those with mercy that are returning to their duty. Then set out the prediction given her for comfort in her present distress. Notice is taken of her condition, behold, thou art with child, and therefore this is not a fit place for thee to be in; and it is a great comfort to women with child to think that they are under the particular cognizance and care of divine providence, since God graciously considers their case and suits supports to it. The angel assures her of a safe delivery, and of a son, which Abram desired; this fright and ramble of hers might have destroyed her hope of an offspring, but God dealt not with her according to her folly, and she was saved in child-bearing, not only by providence but by promise. And he names her child, which was an honour both to her and to it: call him Ishmael, God will hear, and the reason is because the Lord has heard — he has, and therefore he will.

Say this mode of address is used to show her that she was known, and to remind her that she was the property of another; and that it is a check to her pride, for though she was Abram’s wife he calls her Sarai’s maid to humble her, and a rebuke to her flight, since Sarai’s maid ought to be in Sarai’s tent and not wandering in the wilderness. Take the first question as bidding her consider that she is running away both from the duty she was bound to and the privileges she was blessed with in Abram’s tent; and the second as a warning where she is going, since she is running herself into sin in Egypt, and if she return to that people she will return to their gods. Note that she acknowledges her fault in fleeing, and yet excuses it, that it was from the face, or displeasure, of her mistress. On the command, say, go home and humble thyself for what thou hast done amiss, and resolve for the future to behave thyself better. And on the promise, ask who says this — the person who is called the Angel of the Lord, and he certainly speaks with all the authority which is proper to God; note the doubled Hebrew, multiplying I will multiply it, that is, multiply it in every age so as to perpetuate it; and add that it is supposed the Turks at this day are descended from Ishmael, and they are a great people.

debates: Whether Sarai had actually ill-used Hagar or only reduced her rank.
Whether a servant may lawfully escape a harsh master.
How an angel can promise what God alone can perform.
Why the angel asks questions to which the answers are known.
What Hagar gained by returning.
outliers: Ellicott shows that submit thyself and dealt hardly render one Hebrew verb, and concludes there was no maltreatment at all.
Ellicott blames the contrary opinion on commentators reading the English version rather than the Hebrew.
Calvin argues from the verse that harsh masters and unjust rulers are still to be endured, while thanking God that servitude has been abolished.
Ellicott frames the whole episode as an exchange: Hagar accepts slavery so that her son may be free.
Calvin observes that God allures rather than compels, mingling paternal invitations with his commands.
Ellicott notes that God is represented as drawing the story out of the person visited rather than presuming it.
Gill reports and dismisses a rabbinic count of four or five successive angels.

11.pericope_label: And the angel of the Lord said unto her, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the Lord hath heard thy affliction — and he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren

schools.summary: Explain that the angel now unfolds what he had briefly said about her seed, and commences with Ishmael, who was to be its head and origin. Although we shall afterwards see that he was a reprobate, an honourable name is granted him to mark the temporal benefit of which he became a partaker as a son of Abram: God intended that a monument of the paternal kindness with which he embraced the whole house of Abram should endure to posterity, for although the covenant of eternal life did not belong to Ishmael, yet, that he might not be entirely without favour, God constituted him the father of a great and famous people. Thus, with respect to this present life, the goodness of God extended itself to the seed of Abram according to the flesh; and if God intended the name of Ishmael to be a perpetual memorial of his benefits, he will by no means bear with our ingratitude if we do not celebrate his eternal mercies unto death. Note also that we do not read that Hagar, in her difficulties, had recourse to prayer, and are rather left to conjecture that when she was stupefied by her sufferings the angel came of his own accord. There are therefore two ways in which God looks down upon men for the purpose of helping them: either when they, as suppliants, implore his aid, or when he, even unasked, succours them in their afflictions. On the character, reject the exposition that makes the word mean a forester, one addicted to the hunting of wild beasts, since the explanation must be sought in the context and not elsewhere; the simple meaning is that he will be a warlike man, and so formidable to his enemies that none shall injure him with impunity. Then ask whether this ought to be reckoned among benefits conferred by God, that he is to preserve his rank in life by force of arms, seeing that nothing is in itself more desirable than peace. The difficulty may be solved thus: that Ishmael, although all his neighbours should make war upon him and conspire on every side to destroy him, shall yet, though alone, be endued with sufficient power to repel all their attacks. But hold that the angel by no means promises him complete favour, only that which is limited: among our chief blessings we must desire to have peace with all men, and since this is denied to Ishmael, that blessing which is next in order is granted him, namely, that he shall not be overcome by his enemies but shall be brave and powerful to resist their force. He does not speak of Ishmael’s person but of his whole progeny, for what follows is not strictly suitable to one man; and on this exposition no simple or unmixed blessing is here promised, but only a tolerable or moderate condition, so that Ishmael and his posterity might perceive that something was divinely granted to them for the sake of their father Abram. It is by no means to be reckoned among the benefits given by God that he shall have all around him as enemies, and shall resist them all by violence. Elsewhere describe him as living in a wilderness, delighting in hunting, and robbing all that pass by, and his posterity as wild, fierce and untamed, never subdued or brought into bondage by Assyrians, Medes and Persians, Greeks or Romans; note that the Arabs now live independent of the Turks and oblige them to pay a yearly tribute for the passage of their pilgrims to Mecca and for their caravans; and that one Jewish commentator therefore renders the word free.

Derive the name from the verb to hear and the name of God, since the angel says the Lord hath heard thy affliction; and say the name must ever keep the mother in remembrance of God’s merciful interposition in her behalf, and remind the child and the man that he was an object of God’s gracious and providential goodness. Add that afflictions and distresses have a voice in the ears of God even when prayer is restrained, but how much more powerfully do they speak when endured in meekness of spirit, with confidence in and supplication to the Lord. Or say more briefly that the experience we have had of God’s seasonable kindness in distress should encourage us to hope for the like help in the like exigencies, and that even there where there is little cry of devotion, the God of pity hears the cry of affliction, for tears speak as well as prayers. On the character, trace the root to an Arabic verb meaning to run away or run wild, whence the wild ass, from its fleetness and untamable nature; and quote what is said of the wild ass in Job as the very best description that can be given of the Ishmaelites, the wandering Arabs descended from him. God himself has sent them out free and loosed them from all political restraint; the wilderness is their habitation, and in the parched land where no other human beings could live they have their dwellings; they scorn the city and have no fixed habitations; for their multitude they are not afraid, since when they make depredations on towns they retire into the desert so precipitately that all pursuit is eluded, and in this respect the crying of the driver is disregarded; they may be said to have no lands, and yet the range of the mountains is their pasture, for they pitch their tents and feed their flocks wherever they please. Or divide the verse and give its halves different offices: his hand against every man is his sin, and every man’s hand against him is his punishment — those that have turbulent spirits have commonly troublesome lives, and they that are provoking and injurious to others must expect to be repaid in their own coin. And on the last clause say that though threatened and insulted by all his neighbours he shall keep his ground, and, for Abram’s sake more than his own, shall be able to make his part good with them.

Say the name means God heareth, and note that, like Samuel, Ishmael received his name from the events of his mother’s life and not from anything in his own — though there was no rule in this matter, and the naming of children in the Book of Genesis is very diversified. Render the next phrase literally, he will be a wild-ass man, and defend the animal: the wild ass of the Arabian deserts is a very noble creature, and is one of the animals selected in the Book of Job as especially exemplifying the greatness of God. Its characteristics are great speed, love of solitude, and an untamable fondness of liberty; it is thus the very type of the Bedaween Arabs, whose delight is to rove at will over the desert, and who despise the ease and luxury of a settled life. On the following clause, say the Bedaween can be bound by no treaties, submit to no law, and count plunder as legitimate gain. And on the last, give the sense that he shall maintain his independence, and his descendants shall continue to exist as a free race in the presence of the other Abrahamic nations; but report that many commentators consider the more exact rendering to be that he shall dwell to the east of all his brethren, which is certainly the meaning of the word in one later passage, though it does not suit equally well in another.

debates: Whether the wild-ass comparison is a compliment or a reproach.
Whether it is a blessing to be able to resist all comers.
Whether the last clause means in the presence of, or to the east of, his brethren.
Whether God helped Hagar although she had not prayed.
Why a reprobate should be given an honourable name.
outliers: Ellicott and Clarke both make the wild ass a noble figure of liberty; Calvin rejects the animal altogether for a warlike man.
Calvin grades the blessing, allowing Ishmael only the one next after the peace denied him.
Calvin denies outright that having enemies on every side can be counted among God’s benefits.
Wesley assigns the two halves of the verse to sin and to punishment respectively.
Calvin distinguishes two modes of divine help, to the suppliant and to the merely afflicted.
Ellicott reports a rival rendering that turns a promise of survival into a note of geography.
Gill dates the fulfilment to his own century, with the Arabs exacting tribute from the Turks.

13.pericope_label: And she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me? — wherefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi — and Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son’s name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael — and Abram was fourscore and six years old, when Hagar bare Ishmael to Abram

schools.summary: Render it, Thou art a God of seeing — not, as one Aramaic version paraphrases, Thou art a God that sees all things, but Thou art a God that permits himself to be seen; for so Hagar proceeds herself to explain the name, do not I still see after seeing? With all the love of an Oriental for dark sayings she plays upon the word, but her meaning is plain: do I not see, and therefore am alive, and not even blinded, nor bereft of sense and reason, though I have seen God. On the well, give the name as the well of the living-seeing of God, the well where God has been seen and the beholder still lives; note that it became afterwards a favourite dwelling-place of Isaac and was probably therefore surrounded by pastures, though its site has not been identified, and that of the two places named as landmarks the second is absolutely unknown. Elsewhere run the verses through and note that, having returned to Abram’s house, Hagar bore him a son in his eighty-sixth year; that he gave it the name Ishmael, and regarded it probably as the promised seed, until, thirteen years afterwards, the counsel of God was more clearly unfolded to him.

Take it that Hagar, after she was admonished by the angel, changed her mind, and being thus subdued betook herself to prayer; or at least that she who had before been of a wild and intractable temper begins now at length to acknowledge the providence of God. As to the supposition that God is here called the God of vision because he appears and manifests himself to men, call it a forced interpretation; rather understand that Hagar, who before had appeared to herself to be carried away by chance through the desert, now perceives and acknowledges that human affairs are under divine government — and whoever is persuaded that he is looked upon by God must of necessity walk as in his sight. On the well, take the verb indefinitely, as is usual enough in Hebrew, so that it may be resolved into the passive, the well was called; yet think this common appellation originated with Hagar, who, not content with one simple confession, wished that the mercy of God should be attested in time to come, and therefore transmitted her testimony as from hand to hand. Hence we infer how useful it is that they who do not freely humble themselves should be subdued by stripes: Hagar, who had always been wild and rebellious, and who had at length entirely shaken off the yoke, now, when the hardness of her heart was broken by afflictions, appears altogether another person. She was not, however, reduced to order by stripes only, but a celestial vision was also added, which thoroughly arrested her; and the same thing is necessary for us, namely, that God, while chastising us with his hand, should also bring us into a state of submissive meekness by his Spirit. Reject the opinion of some among the Hebrews that the name was given as a testimony of a twofold favour, because Ishmael was revived from death and God had respect to his mother; for they foolishly mutilate things joined together, since Hagar wished to testify that she had been favourably regarded by him who was the Living God, the Author of life. On the naming of the child, note that Hagar had been commanded to give that name, but that the narrative follows the order of nature, because fathers, by the imposition of the name, declare the power which they have over their sons; we may easily gather that Hagar, when she returned home, related the events which had occurred, so that Abram shows himself obedient and grateful to God, both naming his son according to the command of the angel and celebrating the goodness of God in having hearkened to the miseries of Hagar. Elsewhere report the Targums, one making her pray in the name of the Lord, another making her confess or give thanks before the Lord whose Word spake to her, and a third taking in both prayer and praise — in which may be observed the sense of the ancient synagogue, that this angel was the Word of the Lord, the eternal Son of God. And on the well, allow that the name signifies the well of him that liveth and seeth me, that is, of the living and all-seeing God; or that it may have respect to herself, the well of her that liveth and seeth, who had had a sight of God and yet was alive; and note that a Jewish commentator says the well was in his own day called by the name of one near Mecca, which the Arabs say is the well by which Hagar sat down with Ishmael.

Say she invoked the name of the Lord who spake to her, thus: Thou God seest me. She found that the eye of a merciful God had been upon her in all her wanderings and afflictions, and her words seem to intimate that she had been seeking the divine help. Call the last clause of the verse very obscure, rendered differently by all the versions; the general sense taken out of it is that Hagar was now convinced God himself had appeared to her, and was surprised to find that notwithstanding this she was still permitted to live, since it is generally supposed that if God appeared to any they must be consumed by his glories. But since the word which we render simply after in other places signifies the latter days or after times, it may probably have a similar meaning here, and indeed this makes a consistent sense: have I here also seen the latter purposes or designs of him who seeth me? — an exclamation which may be referred to the discovery God had just made of the future state of her descendants. Or expound it devotionally: thus she made confession of his name, and this should be his name for ever with her, and this his memorial, by which she will know and remember him while she lives. Thou seest my sorrow and affliction, which Hagar especially refers to, for when we have brought ourselves into distress by our own folly yet God has not forsaken us; thou seest the sincerity of my repentance; thou seest me, if in any instance I depart from thee — and this thought should always restrain us from sin and excite us to duty. Add that probably she knew not who it was that talked with her till he was departing, and then looked after him. On the well, say that to commemorate the wonderful discovery God had made of himself she called it a well to the Living One who seeth me, and that two things seem implied: a dedication of the well to him who had appeared to her, and faith in the promise, for he who is the Living One, existing in all generations, must have it ever in his power to accomplish promises which are to be fulfilled through the whole lapse of time. Note also that this was the place where the God of glory manifested the special care he took of a poor woman in distress, and that those who are graciously admitted into communion with God, and receive seasonable comforts from him, should tell others what he has done for their souls, that they also may be encouraged to seek him and trust in him. And on the birth, ask why Abram is blamed: God had not as yet told him how he was to have an heir, the promise saying simply that he who should come forth out of his own bowels should be his heir, and concubinage under that dispensation was perfectly lawful; add that Ishmael is the first man in the world whose name was given him of God before he was born.

Take it for granted, though it is not expressly recorded, that Hagar did as the angel commanded her, returning to her mistress and submitting herself, and that then, in the fulness of time, she brought forth her son — for those who obey divine precepts shall have the comfort of divine promises. Then read the birth through the apostle: this was the son of the bondwoman that was born after the flesh, representing the unbelieving Jews. Note first that many who can call Abraham father are yet born after the flesh; and second, that the carnal seed in the church are sooner brought forth than the spiritual, since it is an easier thing to persuade men to assume the form of godliness than to submit to the power of godliness.

debates: What the name Hagar gives to God actually means.
What her closing question asks, and whether it is about survival or about the future.
Whether the well was named by Hagar or by others after her.
Whether Abram is to be blamed for the whole affair.
Whether the vision or the affliction changed Hagar.
outliers: Ellicott makes the name mean a God who permits himself to be seen, against the paraphrase that makes it a God who sees all.
Clarke proposes a rendering that turns the question from Hagar’s survival to the latter purposes of God.
Calvin calls the God of vision reading forced; the editorial matter printed with him lists seven authorities against him.
Calvin makes Hagar’s change the proof that stripes are useful, then insists a vision was needed as well.
Clarke defends Abram on the ground that the manner of the promise had not yet been revealed to him.
Henry reads the birth as the type of a carnal seed brought forth in the church sooner than the spiritual.
Keil and Delitzsch suggest Abram took Ishmael for the promised seed for thirteen years.
